# Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML {#sec-data-efficiency}

**On the wings, GeoTransolver and Transolver are more accurate than ISLA
at every training-set size measured, by 12 to 32% against the reference
configuration.** The ladder below trains every architecture on nested
subsets of HiLiftAeroML, from 35 to 510 cases, and on two further ladders
that vary what the training set contains rather than how large it is, and
scores them all on the same validation cases with the same instrument. The
ordering never changes. What the chapter adds beyond the ordering is
*where* ISLA's error comes from on this dataset: it is paid in distinct
geometries rather than cases, it concentrates in the slat and flap gaps,
and it is representational rather than a data limit. The single-factor
ablation at the end prices each of ISLA's ingredients. Every ISLA number in
this chapter's figures and tables is ISLA unless a
collapsed note says otherwise.

Two conventions hold throughout, as everywhere in the book: the metric is
the area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure in float32 (@sec-metrics),
and a ratio between architectures is baseline error divided by ISLA error,
so a value above one would favor ISLA.

```{python}
#| label: setup-de
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
```

## What was measured {#sec-de-setup}

HiLiftAeroML (@sec-datasets) holds 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing
geometries, each simulated at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°. Three
ladders are used here.

- **The case ladder.** Nested random draws of 35, 210, 510 and 1,260
  training cases from a 1,260-case pool, sharing one 180-case validation set
  (@sec-splits). The validation geometries recur in training at other
  angles. The 35-case draw contains 33 distinct geometries and no case at
  18°.
- **The geometry ladder.** 40 cases on 4 geometries and 210 cases on 21
  geometries, each at all ten angles, validated on 180 cases of 18
  geometries that appear in no training set.
- **The fixed-angle split.** 126 geometries at 12°, validated on 18 held-out
  geometries at the same angle.

Every architecture trains under the frozen protocol (@sec-protocol): 10,000
sampled surface points per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16, no augmentation, two
or three seeds, the freestream as a unit direction, and the learning rate
each architecture prefers on the full split (ISLA 1e-3, Transolver 3e-3,
GeoTransolver 1e-3 except at 35 cases, where its 3e-3 lane is better and is
the one reported). Every number is a float32 evaluation of the final-epoch
checkpoint; no checkpoint is selected on validation error. Parameters are
matched (ISLA 8.9M, GeoTransolver 9.0M, Transolver 6.0M) and so are tokens
per case; the step cost is in @sec-cost.

ISLA is the shipped configuration (relative frame, total-measure length unit;
@sec-mt2), measured on the 35-case, 210-case, 4-geometry, 21-geometry and
fixed-angle rungs. It is not yet trained on the 510- and 1,260-case rungs,
which the scoreboard lists among the measurements still to be made
(@sec-scoreboard).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why every model receives the freestream as a unit direction"}
Fed the physical freestream velocity of 2,679.5 in/s instead, GeoTransolver's
global-context projector collapses to one occupied slice per head and both
baselines lose 3.4 to 3.8x at 35 cases. The mechanism, the control that
established it and the resulting protocol rule are in @sec-part-baseline;
every number in this chapter is a unit-direction number.
:::

## The ladder {#sec-de-result}

**Both baselines are more accurate than ISLA on every rung measured:
baseline ÷ ISLA lies between 0.68 and 0.88.**

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-ladder

def cell(v):
    if not v:
        return "not trained"
    m = statistics.mean(v)
    return f"{m:.4f} ({min(v):.4f}–{max(v):.4f})" if len(v) > 1 else f"{m:.4f}"
def ratio(a, b):
    return f"{statistics.mean(a) / statistics.mean(b):.2f}" if a and b else "—"
print("| rung | GeoTransolver | Transolver | ISLA | GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA | Transolver ÷ ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|")
for name in ("35 cases", "210 cases", "4 geometries", "21 geometries", "fixed angle"):
    r = LADDER[name]
    print(f"| {name} | {cell(r['gt'])} | {cell(r['t'])} | **{cell(r['isla_ref'])}** | "
          f"{ratio(r['gt'], r['isla_ref'])} | {ratio(r['t'], r['isla_ref'])} |")
print()
print(": The HiLiftAeroML ladders in float32: seed mean (seed range) of surface-pressure error on the shared validation cases, and each baseline's mean divided by ISLA's (below one means the baseline is more accurate). GeoTransolver at learning rate 3e-3 at 35 cases and 1e-3 elsewhere; Transolver at 3e-3; ISLA at 1e-3. The 510- and 1,260-case rungs await ISLA (@sec-scoreboard). Same sources as @fig-hilift-data-efficiency. {#tbl-hilift-ladder}")
```

The preregistered bar for an ISLA advantage, baseline ÷ ISLA of at least
1.10 with ISLA lower on two thirds of the cases, is approached on no rung.
At 35 cases and at the fixed angle the baselines lead on velocity and wall
shear as well as pressure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Case-by-case counts and the frame price (diagnostic, legacy centered variant)"}
The program's earlier configuration, the legacy centered variant (plain-mean
center, constant length unit; @sec-mt2-variants), was measured on every
rung, and the per-case counts were reduced against it: at 210 cases
GeoTransolver is lower on 161 of 180 validation cases and Transolver on
149; at 510 cases both on 168 of 180; at 21 geometries on 136 and 135; at
the fixed angle on all 18 held-out geometries. At 4 geometries the mean and
the count disagree: GeoTransolver is 0.76x by the mean but lower on only 96
of 180 cases and 9 of 18 geometries, because a tail of geometries on which
ISLA is up to twice as bad carries the mean.

ISLA pays a price against that variant that depends
on whether validation geometries recur in training: 11% at 35 and 210
cases, where every validation geometry appears in training at other
angles; 1% and 5% on the two never-seen-geometry rungs; 14% at the fixed
angle; nothing on DrivAerML. The price is a mesher pattern, not lost
position: on the 35-case and fixed-angle splits a diagnostic ISLA handed the
exact frame of the full geometry as global data, so lacking no positional
information, paid as much or more (14 to 16% and 21%). What the plain-mean
centroid reads is where the mesher placed its cells, which displaces that
centroid by 0.131 body lengths on these wings and 0.034 on DrivAerML cars,
a reusable cue exactly when the same geometries recur or a single angle
fixes the refinement pattern. That content is discretization-dependent and
ISLA declines to carry it (@sec-principle); the
consistency benchmark of @sec-consistency-bench is where it earns its price.
Data: results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json,
results/udrvl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json,
results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json.
:::

## Controls {#sec-de-controls}

**The two-seed spread at small rungs understates the uncertainty by a
factor of three to eleven; the training draw is the larger source, and the
ordering holds on every draw.** The 35-case split is one random draw from
the pool. Re-running GeoTransolver, Transolver and ISLA (its legacy centered
variant stood in for ISLA in this control; the interval is a property of
the draw, not of the configuration) on three further geometry-stratified
35-case draws, three seeds each, gives GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA between 0.88
and 0.96 across draws (mean
0.91, 90% interval 0.84 to 0.98) and Transolver ÷ ISLA between 0.85 and
0.90 (mean 0.87, interval 0.82 to 0.92); the curated draw is typical for
every arm. At 210 cases the same design gives 0.87 (0.82 to 0.93) and 0.90
(0.85 to 0.95). Every 35-case and 210-case ratio in the book is to be read
with these intervals, which are the bars in the scoreboard's forest plot
(@sec-scoreboard). Data:
research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n35_fp32_2026-09-10.json
and campaign_a_n210_fp32_2026-09-10.json.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The other steel-man controls"}
- **Learning rate.** At 35 cases GeoTransolver at 3e-3 beats its 1e-3 lane
  on 158 of 180 cases and is the lane reported; at every other rung 1e-3 is
  better. Transolver at 1e-3 is worse than at 3e-3 at 35 cases and stays at
  3e-3.
- **Seeds.** Third seeds at 35 and 210 cases move neither baseline's mean by
  more than 0.001.
- **The surface measure.** Giving GeoTransolver and Transolver the same
  quadrature measure ISLA carries, in their slice pooling, costs them 6.5% at
  35 cases and leaves them ahead of ISLA. These measure-weighted baselines
  are ablations that locate a property, not modifications of the
  public models.
- **ISLA's own controls** are the single-factor ablations of @sec-mechanism.

Data: results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json,
results/mw_w4dr_xfam_reduction_2026-09-10.json.
:::

## What ISLA's error responds to {#sec-de-strata}

**ISLA's error is paid for in geometries, not cases; it tracks the flow
physics case by case; and the deficit to the baselines is
representational.** Three observations about ISLA alone.

*Geometry count.* Cutting the training geometries six- to eight-fold at a
similar case count (4 geometries at ten angles against 35 cases on 33
geometries; 21 geometries against 210 cases on about 126) costs ISLA 1.5 to
1.8x. The comparison changes the validation population as well as the
training composition, so it supports a geometry-count reading and not the
stronger statement that geometry count alone sets the error.

*Flow difficulty.* ISLA's error is about twice as large post-stall as in
attached flow, it interpolates smoothly at the one angle absent from
training, and its residual concentrates where the geometry is intricate:
the slat and flap gaps hold about 15% of the sampled points and most of the
squared error. The per-band table is in the collapsed note below.

*Capacity.* Trained and evaluated on one case at a time (64 sampled views of
a single wing), ISLA's one-car floor, the converged error on a single
training case, is 1.27x GeoTransolver's and 1.37x Transolver's, wider than
the 35-case gap, and the deficit sits on the smooth, large-cell open
surfaces rather than at the gaps. A deficit that widens when the data are
held fixed is not a data limit; it is representational, and the DrivAerML
anatomy of @sec-deficit-anatomy locates it
(results/overfit_single_case_2026-09-11.json).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The per-band residual and the seen-geometry effect (diagnostic, legacy centered variant)"}
These three measurements were made on the legacy centered variant. On the
35-case split its error is 0.09 to 0.10 in attached flow (4° to 12°) and
0.17 to 0.19 post-stall, and its per-case error rises with angle of attack
(rank correlation 0.56 at 35 cases, 0.61 at 210). Seeing a geometry at
another angle helps it by 15% at 35 cases
(results/hilift_seen_vs_unseen_geometry_2026-09-07.json).

| training cases | near band (0.7–2% chord), about 15% of points | 2–10% of chord, about 6% of points | open surface (>10%), about 79% of points |
|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | 59% | 4% | 36% |
| 210 | 71% | 4% | 23% |

: Where ISLA's residual pressure error lives on the 35- and 210-case splits (legacy centered variant, two-seed mean predictions, median over the 180 validation cases): the share of ISLA's squared error in each band of distance to the nearest facing surface, with the median share of sampled points each band holds. The facing-surface distance is the local gap or cove width and is infinite on an open convex surface. Data: results/hlreg_facing_distance_35_2026-09-08.json, results/hlreg_facing_distance_210_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-hilift-hlreg}
:::

## In engineering terms: lift and drag {#sec-de-forces}

From a few dozen CFD runs ISLA predicts the integrated lift and drag
coefficients of the validation cases to a few percent, and from the full
split to about one percent; the baselines' forces are not reduced, so this
is a statement about what a small budget yields from ISLA, not a
comparison.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The force numbers (diagnostic, legacy centered variant)"}
Measured on the legacy centered variant: from 35 CFD runs it predicts the
drag coefficient of the 180 validation cases to 3.3% and the lift
coefficient to 3.0% (mean absolute error relative to the mean magnitude),
and from 1,260 to 1.4% and 0.9%
(results/hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json). The reference is the CFD
label integrated on the same 10,000 sampled cells as the prediction, so the
sampling error of the integral cancels; how far a 10,000-cell integral sits
from the full-surface force is not measured.
:::

## A free uncertainty signal {#sec-de-uq}

The disagreement between a model's two seeds ranks its per-case error at
small training sets, so a two-seed ISLA ships with a usable per-case
confidence flag from 35 cases; the ranking is tested, not calibration, and
the same signal is not measured for the baselines.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The correlations (diagnostic, legacy centered variant)"}
For the legacy centered variant the Spearman correlation between two-seed
disagreement and per-case error is +0.67 at 35 cases, about +0.6 at 210,
and +0.15 at 1,260, where seed disagreement no longer predicts error
(@sec-shared-floor). Two-seed ensembles gain only 1 to 5%
(results/hilift_ensemble_uq_{35,210,1260}_2026-09-06.json).
:::

## What each ingredient costs ISLA {#sec-mechanism}

**No single ingredient moves ISLA's error by more than 16%: the relational
invariants are the largest single ingredient, and the measure weights cost
in distribution as an estimator-variance effect that shrinks with cell
count.** The single-factor ablation that established this was run on the
program's earlier configuration, the legacy centered variant, at 35 cases;
its table and the measure-weight decomposition are in the collapsed note.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The single-factor ablation and the price of the measure weights (diagnostic, legacy centered variant)"}
Removing one ingredient at a time from the legacy centered variant at 35
cases gives @tbl-hilift-ablations.

| single-factor change to the legacy centered variant at 35 cases | error (seed 42 / 43) | ÷ 0.138 |
|---|---|---|
| add raw coordinates as inputs (breaks exact equivariance) | 0.143 / 0.143 | 1.04x |
| replace the invariant seeds by the raw vectors | 0.138 / 0.137 | 0.99x |
| similarity gauge on | 0.151 / 0.147 | 1.08x |
| measure weights off (ablation, not adopted) | 0.121 / 0.123 | **0.88x** |
| relational invariants off in routing and read-back | 0.158 / 0.163 | 1.16x |

: Single-factor ablations of ISLA's legacy centered variant at 35 training cases, two seeds, frozen protocol, shared validation set; greater than one means worse. Every variant retains an invariant path somewhere, so these results speak to exactness and to individual ingredients, not to the presence of invariant information. Data: results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-05.json. {#tbl-hilift-ablations}

Exactness of the equivariance is not load-bearing in distribution (raw
coordinates cost 4%); the invariant seed set is not (raw vectors cost
nothing); the similarity gauge costs 8% at this rung; the relational
invariants are worth 16%.

**Measure weights are a correctness requirement, and their in-distribution
price is known.** Turning them off improves the legacy centered variant by
12% at 35 cases, 8% at 210, 17% at 4 geometries, 11% at 21, 11% at the
fixed angle, and 3% on DrivAerML. The price has two parts. One is estimator
variance: with the weights on, the effective number of tokens per slice is
about a fifth of the count, and on DrivAerML the weights-off advantage
shrinks from 11% at 2,500 cells to 2.4% at 40,000. The other, on the
wings, is mesh-pattern content: there the advantage is flat at 12 to 13%
from 2,500 to 40,000 cells, which variance cannot be, and under
area-proportional resampling it inverts, the weights-off model's error
rising above that of predicting zero while the weighted model's falls with
count (@sec-consistency-bench). A configuration that reads the mesher's
cell placement is not a surrogate for the surface (@sec-principle); the
weights-off ISLA is an ablation and never a configuration. Data:
results/nowl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/geo210_all_arms_2026-09-10.json,
results/now_single12_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json.
:::

## The same protocol on DrivAerML {#sec-de-drivaerml}

**There is no ISLA advantage on DrivAerML at any training-set size
either.** The DrivAerML ladder was run on the legacy centered variant; the
ISLA is trained on DrivAerML only at 435 cars, where the
float32 standing is in @sec-full-data-accuracy. From 27 cars up
GeoTransolver is 1.2 to 1.3x more accurate than that variant, and the
deficit is uniform in every way measured.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The DrivAerML ladder (diagnostic, legacy centered variant)"}
The ladder trains on nested subsets of the 435-car training split at
learning rate 3e-3 for both architectures, 500 epochs, 10,000 tokens, two
seeds, scored on the 48 validation cars in bfloat16 on identical points.
GeoTransolver's ladder lanes received the freestream as a physical velocity,
which on this dataset costs it nothing (within a percent of the unit
direction at 435 cars in float32, @sec-full-data-accuracy), so the ordering
is read as it stands.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
lad = json.load(open(RES / "ladder_reduction.json"))
print("| training cars | GeoTransolver | ISLA, legacy centered variant | GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---:|")
for n in (14, 27, 54, 109, 218):
    g = [lad[f"lad_gt_n{n}_seed{s}"]["infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
    m = [lad[f"lad_mt2_n{n}_seed{s}"]["infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
    gm, mm = statistics.mean(g), statistics.mean(m)
    print(f"| {n} | {gm:.3f} ({min(g):.3f}–{max(g):.3f}) | {mm:.3f} ({min(m):.3f}–{max(m):.3f}) | {gm/mm:.2f} |")
print()
print(": DrivAerML data-efficiency ladder: surface-pressure error on the 48 validation cars, seed mean (seed range), learning rate 3e-3 for both architectures (ISLA's preferred 1e-3 is worth about 1.1x at full data and does not change the ordering). ISLA is the legacy centered variant; ISLA is trained on DrivAerML only at 435 cars (@sec-full-data-accuracy). Bfloat16 evaluation on identical points; the float32 offset on this dataset moves every close comparison toward GeoTransolver. Data: results/ladder_reduction.json. {#tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder}")
```

At 14 cars the two tie; from 27 cars up GeoTransolver is 1.2 to 1.3x more
accurate. The deficit is uniform in every way measured: the same on every
third of the car, a near-constant factor per car on a difficulty ordering
both architectures share (per-case rank correlation 0.86 to 0.89, equal to
each architecture's correlation with its own second seed), and the same for
the surface and the volume
(results/drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json).
:::

## Limits of the claim {#sec-de-limits}

- **The ladder is a data-efficiency measurement, not a scaling law.** ISLA's
  log-log slope of error against training cases (measured on the legacy
  centered variant, which spans four rungs) flattens from 0.42 to 0.31 to
  0.21 over the three segments, and the baselines' curves are flat in ratio
  to it. Three observations suggest the
  flattening is a floor of the protocol rather than a property of ISLA
  (@sec-shared-floor); that reading is a hypothesis.
- **It is in-distribution and a validation-set figure.** The validation
  cases share the training design; the checkpoints are final-epoch with no
  selection, but the validation set was reused adaptively for the baselines'
  per-rung learning rate and for what to present, and the sealed test was
  spent on regime extrapolation (@sec-limits-validation). Across a regime
  boundary no architecture generalizes (@sec-regime-extrapolation).
- **Seeds do not measure the choice of training cases.** The draw intervals
  of @sec-de-controls are the uncertainty to read, and they exist only at 35
  and 210 cases.
- **No mechanism of an ISLA accuracy advantage is established, because no
  such advantage is established.** What ISLA buys is stated elsewhere: exact
  pose covariance (@sec-pose-contract), a frame that converges under
  refinement (@sec-consistency-bench), and the interior velocity lead
  (@sec-interior).
